name: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree

clinicalPearls: Liver cancer is the sixth most common cancer worldwide and the third leading cause of cancer-related death; hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) makes up about 85% of primary liver cancers, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma about 10%, with rarer entities including fibrolamellar HCC, mixed HCC-iCCA, epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, and pediatric hepatoblastoma (Harrison 22e p.659).

Cirrhosis of any cause is the dominant risk factor for HCC; about one-third of cirrhotic patients develop HCC over their lifetime, with an annual risk of roughly 3-8% in HBV- or HCV-related cirrhosis and a lower 1-2% per year in cirrhosis from alcohol, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson's disease, and cholestatic disorders (Harrison 22e p.659-660).

HBV accounts for roughly 50% of HCC cases globally (about 60% in Asia and Africa, about 20% in the West) and can cause tumors via insertional mutagenesis; importantly, 25-30% of MASH-associated HCCs arise in the absence of cirrhosis (Harrison 22e p.660).

HCC has a strong male preponderance (male-to-female ratio about 2.5:1) and incidence peaks at 65-70 years, though it presents earlier (40-50 years) in populations with vertical HBV transmission (Harrison 22e p.659).

The radiologic hallmark of HCC on four-phase CT or dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI is arterial-phase contrast uptake with washout in the portal venous or delayed phase, a pattern with about 95-100% specificity that can make biopsy unnecessary in cirrhotic patients (Harrison 22e p.661).

The Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) system is the most accepted staging scheme; the TNM staging system is NOT used in HCC because it does not capture liver function and performance status, the key prognostic variables (Harrison 22e p.662-664).

Cholangiocarcinoma is the second most common primary liver cancer and is classified by location into intrahepatic (iCCA, ~20-30%), perihilar (pCCA, ~50-60%), and distal (dCCA, ~20-30%); perihilar and distal forms together are termed extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (Harrison 22e p.667).

FGFR2 fusions and IDH1/2 mutations occur mostly in iCCA, whereas ERBB2/3 amplifications and SMAD4 aberrations characterize extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma; up to about 40% of iCCAs carry a targetable mutation (Harrison 22e p.667).

Acute painless jaundice occurs in about 90% of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma patients, while roughly 10% present with cholangitis; distal cholangiocarcinoma can be hard to distinguish from early pancreatic cancer (Harrison 22e p.668-669).

Gallbladder cancer is the most common biliary tract malignancy worldwide, has a female-to-male ratio of about 3:1, and cholelithiasis is the major risk factor though fewer than 1% of patients with gallstones develop it; gallbladder polyps 10 mm or larger carry transformation risk (Harrison 22e p.669-670).

Fibrolamellar HCC typically affects children and young adults (10-30 years) without underlying liver disease, carries the PRKACA-DNAJB1 fusion oncogene in 80-100% of cases, and has a better prognosis than conventional HCC (Harrison 22e p.670).

Hepatic (hepatocellular) adenomas occur predominantly in women aged 35-40 (female-to-male ratio ~10:1), are linked to oral contraceptive use in women and anabolic androgenic steroid use in male bodybuilders, and carry risk of hemorrhage and malignant transformation, particularly when larger than 5 cm (Harrison 22e p.670).
harrison.pathophysiology: HCC develops through a multistep process beginning with precancerous low-grade dysplastic nodules that progress to high-grade dysplastic nodules and then early HCC; adult hepatocytes are the principal cell of origin, either transforming directly or de-differentiating into precursor cells, with progenitor cells contributing in a subset. It is a prototypical inflammation-associated cancer in which oxidative stress and the immune microenvironment of chronically damaged liver drive mutation. Tumors accumulate roughly 40-60 somatic alterations, of which 4-8 are driver genes; the leading drivers are TERT promoter mutations (~56%), TP53 (~27%), and CTNNB1 (~26%), all currently non-actionable. Aflatoxin B1 produces a characteristic TP53 R249S hotspot mutation. Only about 20-25% of HCCs carry an actionable mutation. Two molecular subclasses exist: a proliferative class (poor outcome, HBV-related, AFP overexpression, Ras/mTOR/IGF activation) and a nonproliferative class (often CTNNB1-mutated, better outcome). Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma arises from adult cholangiocytes, transdifferentiated hepatocytes, or progenitor-cholangiocyte precursors, whereas extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma arises from biliary epithelium and peribiliary glands. Hepatic adenomas are clonal proliferations from single-gene driver mutations (e.g., CTNNB1, HNF1A inactivation, inflammatory or Hedgehog pathway activation), and focal nodular hyperplasia is a polyclonal hepatocellular proliferation secondary to an arterial malformation (Harrison 22e p.660-670).
additionalDifferentials: Low-grade and high-grade dysplastic nodules versus early HCC in a cirrhotic liver
Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma versus metastatic adenocarcinoma (colorectal, breast, lung) versus mixed HCC-iCCA
Distal cholangiocarcinoma versus early pancreatic cancer
Benign liver lesions: hemangioma, focal nodular hyperplasia, hepatocellular adenoma
additionalInvestigations: Six-monthly abdominal ultrasound with serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) for HCC surveillance in high-risk cirrhotic patients (sensitivity ~65%, specificity >90%)
Four-phase contrast-enhanced CT or dynamic/gadoxetic-enhanced MRI for noninvasive HCC diagnosis using the arterial uptake/washout hallmark
LI-RADS categorization of liver nodules (LI-RADS-5 ~95% probability HCC; LI-RADS-4 ~60-70%; LI-RADS-1 0%)

Liver biopsy with hepatopathologist review when noncirrhotic, atypical imaging, or LI-RADS-4; supportive stains GPC3, glutamine synthetase, HSP70, clathrin heavy chain (2 of 4 positive is highly specific for HCC); a negative biopsy does NOT exclude HCC
CA 19-9 (prognostic at cutoffs ~100-129 U/mL for cholangiocarcinoma but poor for early diagnosis, sensitivity/specificity ~60%)
MRI/MRCP and chest-abdomen CT and PET for cholangiocarcinoma staging; PET helps detect occult lymph node metastasis

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography with brushing cytology plus FISH for polysomy in perihilar/distal cholangiocarcinoma (FISH raises cytology sensitivity from ~20% to ~40%); serum IgG4 to exclude IgG4 cholangiopathy
Child-Pugh score (bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time, ascites, encephalopathy) and ECOG performance status for prognostic assessment
redFlags: Symptomatic HCC (malaise, weight loss, anorexia, abdominal discomfort, or signs of liver dysfunction) indicates advanced disease with median survival under 1 year
Macrovascular (portal, hepatic, or branch vein) invasion, lymph node involvement, or extrahepatic spread denotes advanced BCLC C disease
Child-Pugh class C / severe liver dysfunction (BCLC D)
Rising or markedly elevated AFP (>=20 ng/mL prompting imaging; >=400 ng/dL highly suspicious but not diagnostic)
Painless jaundice or cholangitis suggesting biliary tract malignancy
Hepatic adenoma larger than 5 cm (hemorrhage and malignant transformation risk); active adenoma bleeding
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis depends on stage, tumor burden, liver function, and performance status. About 40% of HCC patients are diagnosed at BCLC stage 0 or A and are eligible for potentially curative resection, transplantation, or ablation, with median overall survival beyond 5 years (up to ~10 years after transplantation). Optimal surgical resection candidates have 5-year survival of 60-70% (35-55% in suboptimal candidates); RFA achieves ~60% 5-year survival; liver transplantation within Milan criteria yields 70-80% 5-year survival with ~10-15% recurrence at 5 years. Intermediate-stage (BCLC B) untreated natural history is about 16 months, improved to ~25-30 months with TACE. Symptomatic/advanced disease has median survival under 1 year; end-stage (BCLC D) survival is about 3-6 months. Cholangiocarcinoma overall carries a 5-year survival of about 10%; resectable iCCA single tumors have median survival ~40-50 months. Gallbladder cancer 5-year survival ranges 60-90% in resected localized disease but only ~10-12 months median in advanced disease. Fibrolamellar HCC has better prognosis (median ~70 months after resection). Hepatoblastoma overall 5-year survival is ~70% (50-90% by PRETEXT stage); notably, low AFP (<100 ng/mL) indicates poor prognosis in hepatoblastoma, opposite to HCC.
pitfalls: A negative liver biopsy does NOT exclude HCC; sensitivity falls below 50% for tumors 1-2 cm, and a second biopsy is advised if findings are inconclusive or the lesion grows/changes enhancement
Nodules under 1 cm are unlikely to be HCC and are difficult to diagnose; short-interval ultrasound follow-up (every 3-4 months) is recommended rather than immediate biopsy
PET and contrast-enhanced ultrasound perform poorly for early HCC diagnosis and are not recommended as primary diagnostic tools
An AFP of >=400 ng/dL is highly suspicious but NOT diagnostic of HCC by guidelines
TNM staging should NOT be applied to HCC because it omits liver function and performance status
About 25-30% of MASH-related HCCs occur without cirrhosis, so absence of cirrhosis does not exclude HCC in this group
Surveillance is generally NOT recommended in advanced (Child-Pugh C) cirrhosis since curative therapy is precluded, except for liver transplant waiting-list patients
Liver biopsy carries a ~2-3% risk of complications including tumor seeding and bleeding
harrison.severityClassification: Hepatocellular carcinoma is staged by the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) system into five stages: very early (BCLC 0, single nodule <=2 cm, Child-Pugh A, ECOG 0), early (BCLC A, single or up to three nodules <=3 cm, Child-Pugh A-B, ECOG 0), intermediate (BCLC B, multinodular, Child-Pugh A-B, ECOG 0), advanced (BCLC C, portal/macrovascular invasion, N1 or M1, or ECOG 1-2), and terminal (BCLC D, Child-Pugh C or ECOG >2). Liver function is graded by the Child-Pugh score (classes A-C) and performance by ECOG. Milan criteria (single tumor <=5 cm, or up to three nodules each <=3 cm, no macrovascular invasion or extrahepatic spread) define transplant eligibility. Cholangiocarcinoma is classified anatomically into intrahepatic, perihilar, and distal subtypes; hepatoblastoma uses the PRETEXT (Pretreatment Extent of Tumor) classification (Harrison 22e p.661-669).
management: Stage-directed treatment using the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer framework, with surgical resection, liver transplantation or local ablation for early-stage hepatocellular carcinoma
Transarterial chemoembolisation for intermediate-stage, liver-confined disease
Systemic therapy for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma, either combination immunotherapy (atezolizumab with bevacizumab) or multikinase inhibitors such as sorafenib or lenvatinib
Treatment of the underlying liver disease and its cause, including antiviral therapy for hepatitis B or C and alcohol cessation, with management of cirrhosis and portal hypertension
Surgical resection with lymphadenectomy and gemcitabine-based chemotherapy for cholangiocarcinoma, with endoscopic biliary drainage or stenting for obstructive jaundice
Regular surveillance ultrasound with serum alpha-fetoprotein in at-risk cirrhotic patients to detect tumours at a curable stage
Hepatobiliary multidisciplinary team management with best supportive and palliative care where appropriate
